q: Explain reverse osmosis and spinning cone in the alcohol-management toolkit.
accept: membrane removes water alcohol cone strips volatiles
de-alcoholization concentration techniques
ans: RO: membrane separation (concentrate must or strip alcohol/VA); spinning cone: vacuum-strips volatiles then alcohol, re-blending aromatics
exp: Legal, common, rarely admitted — the orals ask you to explain without sneering.

q: Explain regenerative viticulture in one sentence and name two practices.
accept: soil carbon health cover crops no till compost grazing
building soil biology sequestering carbon
ans: Farming to rebuild soil biology and sequester carbon — no-till, permanent cover crops, compost, integrated grazing
exp: The successor movement to organic and biodynamic certification.

q: Explain the sulfur-dioxide debate at Master level: three functions and the trade-off.
accept: antioxidant antimicrobial antioxidasic versus aromatic muting and health claims
so2 protects but mutes
ans: SO2 is antioxidant, antimicrobial and antioxidasic; the trade-off is aromatic muting, reduced microbial complexity, and consumer perception — against real spoilage risk
exp: 'Low intervention' is a spectrum of risk tolerance, not a moral position.

q: Explain how yeast selection changes a wine's aromatic outcome, with one concrete example.
accept: thiol releasing strains sauvignon aromatic yeasts versus native complexity
commercial strains express different aromas
ans: Strains differ in enzymatic release of bound precursors — e.g., thiol-releasing strains amplify Sauvignon's passionfruit; native populations give slower, more complex, less predictable results
exp: 'Wild versus cultured' is a decision about risk and signature, not purity.

q: Explain the arguments for and against irrigation in fine wine.
accept: control stress versus dilution vigour banned in some aops
precision versus dilution
ans: For: precise stress management, survival in drought, consistent quality. Against: dilution, excess vigour and shallow rooting — hence its prohibition or restriction in many European AOPs
exp: Climate change is forcing the debate open in regions that banned it.

q: Explain phylloxera at Master level: the organism, how it actually kills a vinifera vine, why American rootstock answers it, and what AxR#1 taught California.
accept: daktulosphaira vitifoliae feeds on the roots the galls stay open and secondary infection kills the vine american species resist so we graft and axr1 failed for its vinifera parentage
root louse raises nodosities and tuberosities secondary rot kills the vine grafting onto american rootstock is the cure
the louse opens wounds vinifera cannot close american vitis walls them off
axr1 collapsed in california because vinifera parentage gives tolerance not resistance
phylloxera kills by the infection that follows the feeding not by the feeding itself
ans: Daktulosphaira vitifoliae, a root-feeding aphid relative native to eastern North America. Feeding on vinifera roots raises galls — nodosities on young rootlets, tuberosities on lignified roots — which never callus over. The vine does not die of the feeding: it dies of the secondary fungal and bacterial infection that enters those open wounds, declining over several years. American species (V. riparia, V. rupestris, V. berlandieri) co-evolved with the louse and wall the feeding site off, so vinifera scions are grafted onto rootstocks bred from them. AxR#1 carries vinifera in its parentage through Aramon; it performed in California for decades and then collapsed from the 1980s, proving that vinifera parentage buys tolerance rather than resistance and forcing the replanting of Napa and Sonoma at enormous cost.
exp: Three things separate a Master answer from a textbook one. First, phylloxera does not really kill by feeding — it kills by opening wounds vinifera cannot close, which is why the decline is slow and is so often blamed on something else. Second, hybrid direct producers were the failed alternative to grafting, and their legacy is the hybrid plantings still standing in New York and Ontario. Third, leaf galls are normal on American vines and hybrids and rare on vinifera, so a galled leaf tells you about the plant material rather than announcing a death. Note too that rootstock is now chosen at least as much for drought, active lime and nematode tolerance as for the louse — which is why a grower on ground the insect has never reached may still graft.

q: Closure choice is really a specification of oxygen transmission rate. Talk me through what you would specify for a wine to be drunk inside three years against one built for twenty, and the fault each specification accepts.
accept: oxygen transmission rate is what you specify low and consistent for early drinking and a small steady budget for long ageing
tin lined screwcap for the young wine accepting reduction risk cork or graded technical cork for the long ager accepting taint and variation
you are choosing between reduction risk and taint and variation risk
the screwcap liner sets the otr and saranex breathes more than tin saran
specify a graded technical cork when you want a stated otr instead of cork's lottery
ans: OTR is the number the decision turns on. For the early-drinking wine you want ingress low and above all consistent — a tin/Saran screwcap liner or a low-OTR technical cork holds fruit and thiols — and the fault you accept is reduction, because a wine bottled with sulfur compounds unresolved and no oxygen budget will never clear them; the levers are bottling less reductively or specifying Saranex, which breathes more. For the long-ageing wine you want a small, steady oxygen budget running for decades: a high-grade natural cork, or a graded technical cork bought at a stated OTR, and the faults you accept are the cork's — TCA and the bottle-to-bottle spread that comes with a biological product. No closure is best. You are choosing which fault you would rather explain to a customer, and how much variation you are willing to ship.
exp: The Master-level move is to stop discussing closures as brands and start discussing a number. Micro-agglomerates are sold in grades precisely so a producer can buy an ageing speed rather than accept whichever one the bark supplies. Two consequences reach the floor. A screwcap does not stop a wine ageing — it slows and standardises it, which is why several estates now bottle one cuvée both ways and taste them against each other year by year. And reduction and taint are opposite problems with opposite responses: reduction is the winery's, usually clears with air, a decant or the copper trick, while taint is the closure's, never improves, and gets the bottle replaced and the case checked rather than decanted in hope.

q: Explain acidification and deacidification: the materials used, and how EU law rations them by wine zone.
accept: tartaric acid up to 4 g/l calcium carbonate to deacidify the north enriches the south acidifies
add tartaric acid in warm zones deacidify in cool zones and enrichment excludes acidification in the same wine
enrichment and acidification of the same wine are forbidden
the eu wine zones decide who may chaptalize and who may acidify
zone a to zone c ladder with tartaric acid as the acidifier
ans: Acidification normally means adding tartaric acid — malic, lactic and citric are also permitted, citric constrained by a 1 g/L ceiling in the finished wine — up to a maximum of 4 g/L expressed as tartaric. Deacidification removes acid with calcium carbonate, potassium bicarbonate or potassium tartrate, capped at 1 g/L expressed as tartaric. The EU divides its vineyard into zones A through C: the cool north (A and B) gets the largest enrichment allowances and may deacidify, while the warm south (Zone C) may acidify — with exceptional-year derogations now blurring both edges. The governing principle is that enrichment and acidification of the same product are mutually exclusive: you may not add sugar and acid to the same wine.
exp: Two things to say aloud. First the arithmetic of the ladder — enrichment ceilings fall as you go south, roughly 3% potential alcohol in Zone A, 2% in B and 1.5% in Zone C, because the law was written for a 1970s climate and assumed the south had sugar to spare. That assumption is what warming has broken, hence the pressure for acidification derogations in Zone B. Second, why tartaric is the acid of choice: it is the grape's own acid, microbially stable, and lowers pH efficiently, whereas malic feeds spoilage bacteria unless malolactic conversion is completed, and lactic barely moves pH at all.

q: Quercetin, tartrates, and pinking — sort the harmless from the fault.
accept: all mostly harmless appearance issues
quercetin haze tartrate crystals pinking oxidative blush harmless
ans: All essentially cosmetic: quercetin haze (sun-exposed reds, classically Sangiovese), tartrate 'diamonds', pinking (mild oxidative blush in whites)
exp: The Master answer distinguishes cosmetic from structural faults calmly.

q: 'Mouthfeel' descriptors mapped to chemistry: astringent, hot, unctuous, spritzig.
accept: tannin protein alcohol glycerol sugar co2
astringent tannin hot ethanol unctuous glycerol sugar spritz co2
ans: Astringency: tannin-protein binding; heat: ethanol; unctuousness: glycerol/sugar/lees; spritz: dissolved CO2
exp: Say the compound with the sensation, always.

q: Why does wine taste different at altitude (aircraft)?
accept: low humidity pressure dulls aroma salt sweet perception
dry cabin low pressure suppress volatiles
ans: Low pressure and bone-dry air suppress volatile perception and dull sweet/salt — hence brutal tannin and mute fruit at 35,000 ft
exp: Airlines pour fruit-forward, low-tannin wines by science.

accept: antioxidant preserves thiols
natural antioxidant protects aromatics
ans: A natural grape antioxidant protecting thiols/aromatics — managed via lees, pressing and additions debates
exp: The premox conversation's quieter chemical thread.

q: You have a pale garnet red, high acid, high drying tannin, dried rose and tar. Give your three top calls and the tiebreakers.
accept: nebbiolo xinomavro sangiovese tar roses versus tomato olive
nebbiolo first xinomavro second
ans: Nebbiolo (tar-rose, alcohol warmth), Xinomavro (tomato-olive-oregano), aged Sangiovese (redder fruit, softer tannin) — the non-fruit signature is the tiebreaker
exp: Never call on color alone; the pale-but-tannic trio is the classic trap.

q: A white shows lanolin, beeswax, lemon and toast at low alcohol with no oak evidence. Call it and defend.
accept: hunter valley semillon aged
aged hunter semillon
ans: Aged Hunter Valley Sémillon — toast without oak at ~10.5% is that wine's fingerprint alone
exp: Chenin brings orchard fruit and higher acid; aged Riesling brings petrol.
